stem: A cluster has 12 brokers. A team sets `bootstrap.servers` on its producers to three of them. A colleague says every broker must be listed or the producers can't reach partitions led by the other nine. Who is right?

options.text: The team: `bootstrap.servers` is only used for the initial connection, and the client discovers the full set of brokers from metadata
The colleague: a client only ever connects to the brokers listed in `bootstrap.servers`
The colleague, unless `client.dns.lookup` is set to `use_all_dns_ips`
Neither: the list must contain exactly one broker, the controller

explanation:
From the config reference: `bootstrap.servers` is "used to establish the initial connection to the Kafka cluster. Clients use this list to bootstrap and discover the full set of Kafka brokers... This list does not need to contain the entire set of brokers". Listing more than one broker gives resilience if one is down at startup.

- After bootstrap the client connects directly to whichever broker leads each partition.
- `client.dns.lookup` changes how hostnames resolve, not whether discovery happens.
- Clients don't need to know the controller.

stem: Topic `payments` has 6 partitions. Consumer group `ledger` runs 6 pods and is falling behind, so the team scales it to 10 pods. What happens to throughput?

options.text: No real gain: each partition goes to one consumer in the group, so 4 pods get no partitions
Throughput rises by about two thirds, because partitions are split across the extra pods
The extra pods share partitions and process alternate records
The broker adds 4 partitions to `payments` to match the group size

explanation:
The `KafkaConsumer` Javadoc: partitions are balanced so that "each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group". With 6 partitions, at most 6 consumers do work; the other 4 are idle standbys that take over if a member fails.

To scale further, add partitions (remembering this changes key-to-partition mapping) or make each consumer faster. Kafka never adds partitions on its own, and classic consumer groups don't split a partition across members.

references.title: KafkaConsumer javadoc: consumer groups and topic subscriptions

stem: A Kafka Streams application reads one input topic with 5 partitions and has no repartitioning. It runs as 4 instances, each with `num.stream.threads=2`. How many stream threads have work?

options.text: 5; the other 3 threads are idle because there are only 5 tasks
8; each thread processes a share of every partition
4; Streams runs one active thread per instance
2; only the threads of the first instance get tasks

explanation:
Streams creates one task per input partition, and each task is processed by exactly one thread. The Streams architecture docs: "the maximum parallelism at which your application may run is bounded by the maximum number of stream tasks, which itself is determined by maximum number of partitions of the input topic(s)". 5 partitions give 5 tasks, so 5 of the 8 threads are busy.

- Threads don't share a partition.
- `num.stream.threads` threads all run tasks; there's no one-thread-per-instance limit.
- Tasks are spread across all instances, not packed onto the first.

references.title: Kafka Streams architecture: stream partitions and tasks

stem: Consumers run in three availability zones, and the brokers set `broker.rack` to their zone. To cut cross-zone traffic, the consumers should fetch from a replica in their own zone instead of the leader. What is needed? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set `client.rack` on each consumer to its zone, matching `broker.rack`
Set `replica.selector.class` on the brokers to a rack-aware selector, such as `org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector`
Set `acks=all` on the producers so followers are always up to date
Set `partition.assignment.strategy` to `RangeAssignor`
Nothing; consumers always read from the nearest replica by default

explanation:
Follower fetching (KIP-392) has a client half and a broker half. `client.rack` tells the broker where the consumer is ("It corresponds with the broker config 'broker.rack'"). The broker picks the preferred read replica with `replica.selector.class`, whose default "returns the leader"; a rack-aware selector picks a replica in the client's rack.

- `acks` affects write durability, not where consumers read.
- The assignor decides which consumer gets a partition, not which replica it reads.
- By default consumers read from the leader.

references.title: KIP-392: Allow consumers to fetch from closest replica

stem:
A consumer runs in a Kubernetes pod. When the pod receives `SIGTERM`, it should finish cleanly. Which order is correct?

1. A JVM shutdown hook calls `consumer.wakeup()`
2. The blocked `poll()` in the main thread throws `WakeupException`
3. The poll loop's `finally` block calls `consumer.close()`
4. `close()` commits offsets (if auto-commit is on) and leaves the group
explanation:
`KafkaConsumer` isn't thread safe; `wakeup()` is the one call that "can safely be used from an external thread to interrupt an active operation. In this case, a WakeupException will be thrown from the thread blocking on the operation." The consumer's own thread then exits the loop and calls `close()`, which "will commit the current offsets if possible" when auto-commit is enabled and leaves the group for a dynamic member.

- `poll()` throws only after `wakeup()` is called.
- Calling `close()` from the hook thread while the main thread is in `poll()` breaks the single-thread rule.

stem: A consumer group of 5 pods is restarted one pod at a time on every deploy, and each restart triggers a rebalance. The team sets `group.instance.id` to the pod name (stable across restarts) and raises `session.timeout.ms` above the restart time. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A pod that comes back within `session.timeout.ms` keeps its partitions without a rebalance
Each pod in the group needs a different `group.instance.id`
A static member's `close()` leaves the group immediately, so the next pod gets its partitions
All pods should share one `group.instance.id` so the group sees them as one member
`group.instance.id` replaces `group.id`, which can then be removed

explanation:
With `group.instance.id` set, the consumer is a static member: "only one instance with this ID is allowed in the consumer group at any time. This can be used in combination with a larger session timeout to avoid group rebalances caused by transient unavailability (e.g. process restarts)." The design docs say to set it "to a unique value for each consumer instance under one group".

- `close()` only leaves the group "if the member is dynamic"; a static member stays until its session times out.
- A shared id would make the instances fence each other.
- `group.id` still names the group.

stem: A containerised producer must read its SASL password from the environment variable `KAFKA_PW` instead of a properties file baked into the image. Which client configuration does that?

options.text: `config.providers=env`, `config.providers.env.class=org.apache.kafka.common.config.provider.EnvVarConfigProvider`, and `${env:KAFKA_PW}` as the password value in `sasl.jaas.config`
`sasl.jaas.config=$KAFKA_PW`, which the client expands like a shell
`config.providers=KAFKA_PW`, which reads any variable of that name
Nothing: every client config can be set as an environment variable named `KAFKA_<CONFIG>`

explanation:
`config.providers` lists aliases for `ConfigProvider` classes, each set with `config.providers.<alias>.class`. A value then references a provider with `${<alias>:<key>}`. `EnvVarConfigProvider` reads environment variables, and the docs note it "is useful for configuring applications running in containers". `FileConfigProvider` and `DirectoryConfigProvider` do the same for mounted files and secrets.

- The Java client doesn't do shell expansion of `$VAR`.
- `config.providers` takes provider aliases, not variable names.
- The `KAFKA_<CONFIG>` convention belongs to some Docker images' startup scripts, not to the Java client.

stem: Which pairing of client setting to its deployment purpose is correct?

options.text: `client.id`: names the instance in broker request logs and metrics; `group.instance.id`: static group membership across restarts; `client.rack`: fetch from the nearest replica
`client.id`: static group membership across restarts; `group.instance.id`: names the instance in metrics; `client.rack`: spreads partitions across racks
`client.rack`: names the instance in broker logs; `client.id`: picks the nearest replica; `group.instance.id`: sets the partition count
`group.instance.id`: joins several groups at once; `client.id`: must be unique or the broker rejects the connection; `client.rack`: the broker's rack

explanation:
- `client.id` is "an id string to pass to the server when making requests" so that a "logical application name" appears in server-side request logging; clients also tag their metrics with it. Duplicates are allowed.
- `group.instance.id` makes the consumer a static member, avoiding rebalances on restarts.
- `client.rack` gives the consumer's rack so a rack-aware broker can serve it from a nearby replica.

The other pairings swap these purposes or invent ones none of the settings has.

stem: Brokers are being upgraded to Kafka 4.0. Which client fleet must be upgraded first, because it can't talk to 4.0 brokers at all?

options.text: Producers and consumers on client version 2.0
Consumers on client version 3.7
Streams applications on version 3.9
Producers on client version 3.0

explanation:
The compatibility matrix lists 0.x, 1.x and 2.0 clients as "Not Compatible" with Kafka 4.0, because pre-0.10 protocol versions were removed (KIP-896). 2.1 to 2.8 clients are partially compatible, and all 3.x clients, Streams and Connect are fully compatible.

This is why client rolling upgrades can usually happen one instance at a time: clients and brokers negotiate API versions, so a mixed fleet keeps working as long as each client is within the supported range.
kafkaVersionNote: Kafka 4.0 removed old protocol versions (KIP-896), dropping support for clients 2.0 and older.
